questions.prompt: Place triangle ABC with C at the origin and B at (a, 0), so A = (b cos C, b sin C). Prove that c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C.
questions.prompt_markup: Place triangle ABC with C at the origin and B at (a, 0), so A = (b cos C, b sin C). Prove that c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C.
questions.correct_answer: c² = (b cos C - a)² + (b sin C)² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C
questions.required_method: Use the distance formula for AB and the identity sin²C + cos²C = 1.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: A = (b cos C, b sin C) because CA = b; c² = (b cos C - a)² + b² sin²C; expand: b²cos²C - 2ab cos C + a² + b² sin²C; sin²C + cos²C = 1 gives a² + b² - 2ab cos C.

questions.prompt: Use the Law of Cosines to prove that in triangle ABC, if c² > a² + b², then ∠C is obtuse.
questions.prompt_markup: Use the Law of Cosines to prove that in triangle ABC, if c² > a² + b², then ∠C is obtuse.
questions.correct_answer: cos C = (a² + b² - c²)/(2ab) < 0, so C is between 90° and 180°: obtuse.
questions.required_method: Solve the law for cos C and decide its sign.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: rearrangement; numerator negative and denominator positive; a negative cosine means an obtuse angle (0° < C < 180°).

questions.prompt: Use the Law of Cosines to prove both directions: in triangle ABC, ∠C = 90° if and only if c² = a² + b².
questions.prompt_markup: Use the Law of Cosines to prove both directions: in triangle ABC, ∠C = 90° if and only if c² = a² + b².
questions.correct_answer: C = 90° gives c² = a² + b²; c² = a² + b² gives cos C = 0, so C = 90°.
questions.required_method: Substitute cos 90° = 0 for one direction; for the converse solve for cos C.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: cos 90° = 0; converse: cos C = 0 with 0° < C < 180° forces C = 90°.
